implementation_notes: The endpoint becomes a worker thread around Thread::Queue: producers push, the worker pops (blocking) and calls the service - a block is the handler, so no adapter class is required. SizedQueue adds the backpressure the plain queue lacks, and a Sidekiq-style worker class is the brokered equivalent where the framework owns acknowledgement and retries. The classic structure is justified only when one queue dispatches to several services by message type. Because the GVL serialises Ruby-level execution, CPU-bound services should scale with processes rather than threads.
code_sketch:
q = Thread::Queue.new
worker = Thread.new do
  loop do
    msg = q.pop                       # blocks until a message arrives
    begin
      out.push(service.call(msg.payload))
    rescue StandardError => e
      errors.push([msg, e])           # never let the worker thread die silently
    end
  end
end
pitfalls: An unhandled exception raised inside a thread terminates that thread without propagating; unless each message is rescued, the queue silently fills while producers keep pushing.
The worker's block closes over its binding: a service or connection captured from a request scope must not be shared with a long-lived worker thread.
Stopping a worker requires an explicit poison value or a closed queue; Thread#kill interrupts at arbitrary points and can abandon half-processed messages.
